subject: Reasoning
description: Mathematical operations / symbol-substitution reasoning: BODMAS application after symbol redefinition, sign-conversion problems.

questions.stem: If '+' means '×', '×' means '÷', '÷' means '−', and '−' means '+', then the value of: 16 + 4 × 2 ÷ 6 − 3 = ?
questions.explanation: STEP 1 — substitute symbols: '+' → ×, '×' → ÷, '÷' → −, '−' → +. So 16 + 4 × 2 ÷ 6 − 3 becomes 16 × 4 ÷ 2 − 6 + 3. STEP 2 — apply real BODMAS: ÷ first, then ×, then +/−. 16 × 4 ÷ 2 = 16 × 2 = 32; then 32 − 6 + 3 = 29. KEY INSIGHT: substitute FIRST, then BODMAS — never mix the two steps. EXAM TRAP: students apply BODMAS to the GIVEN expression with old symbols, then substitute — wrong answer guaranteed. PYQ FREQUENCY: appears 1-2× per year in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC. SHORTCUT: write the converted expression cleanly on rough paper before computing — fewer sign errors. EXAMINER MINDSET: the test isn't arithmetic — it's whether you can hold a substitution rule in working memory while doing real math. CGL & RRB favour 4-symbol redefinitions; SBI PO sometimes uses 5.

questions.stem: If A means '−', B means '×', C means '÷', D means '+', then 18 C 6 D 3 B 4 A 2 = ?
questions.explanation: Substitute letters: A→−, B→×, C→÷, D→+. Expression becomes: 18 ÷ 6 + 3 × 4 − 2. Apply BODMAS: ÷ and × first → 18÷6 = 3; 3×4 = 12. Now: 3 + 12 − 2 = 13. INSIGHT: the trickiest part is keeping track of operator priority AFTER substitution. Letter-substitution problems test attention more than arithmetic. SCAN PATTERN: read left to right, mentally swap each letter for its symbol, write down the cleaner expression, then compute. PYQ ANGLE: SSC CGL and CHSL repeatedly use this letter-pattern (often A,B,C,D = +,−,×,÷ in some permuted order). REASONING SECTION TIP: these are 'free marks' — under 30 seconds with practice. EXAMINER LOGIC: this category tests substitution-and-apply, a core algorithmic skill needed in coding, accounting, and process audits.

questions.stem: If P denotes '÷', Q denotes '×', R denotes '+', S denotes '−', then 36 P 4 Q 5 R 7 S 8 = ?
questions.explanation: Substitute: P→÷, Q→×, R→+, S→−. Expression: 36 ÷ 4 × 5 + 7 − 8. BODMAS — ÷ and × left to right (same priority): 36÷4 = 9; 9×5 = 45. Then 45 + 7 − 8 = 44. KEY RULE: when ÷ and × appear consecutively, evaluate LEFT to RIGHT — they have EQUAL precedence. Same for + and −. INSIGHT: many students wrongly apply ÷ FIRST then × (assuming ÷ outranks ×) — both have equal precedence, so order matters. Compute LTR. NUMERICAL TRICK: 36÷4 = 9 instantly recognizable from times-tables; if you panicked on this, drill 12×12 multiplication tables again. EXAM-FAVORITE for SSC CGL Tier 1 (2-3 such Qs per shift). EXAMINER MINDSET: testing operator precedence + substitution discipline — both core programming skills.

questions.explanation: STEP 1 — substitute: '+' → −, '−' → ×, '×' → ÷, '÷' → +. So 24 ÷ 8 + 6 × 3 − 4 becomes 24 + 8 − 6 ÷ 3 × 4. STEP 2 — apply real BODMAS on the converted expression. ÷ and × together, evaluated LEFT-TO-RIGHT (equal precedence): 6 ÷ 3 = 2; then 2 × 4 = 8. So expression reduces to 24 + 8 − 8 = 24. KEY RULE: ÷ and × have equal precedence and are computed LTR; same for + and −. EXAM TRAP: students isolate 6÷3 alone (= 2), then plug back as 24+8−2 = 30 — that's WRONG because the ×4 must also be processed in the same ÷×-block. CORRECT FLOW: collapse the entire ÷× chain first, then handle +−. PYQ FREQUENCY: this 'compound ÷×' style is a standard CGL/CHSL trap to test BODMAS rigour. EXAMINER MINDSET: verifying you don't 'cherry-pick' operations.

questions.stem: If '+' and '×' are interchanged, what is the value of 4 + 5 × 2 − 3?
questions.explanation: STEP 1 — swap '+' and '×': expression becomes 4 × 5 + 2 − 3. STEP 2 — apply BODMAS on the swapped form: × first → 4×5 = 20. Then 20 + 2 − 3 = 19. KEY METHOD: with a single swap, just rewrite the expression with the two operators exchanged, then compute normally with BODMAS. EXAM TRAP: students apply BODMAS to the ORIGINAL form (4 + 5×2 − 3 = 11) and pick that — wrong because the swap converts the expression. CORRECT SEQUENCE: SWAP first, then BODMAS. PYQ ANGLE: every SSC CGL Tier 1 has 1-2 such swap problems; they're 'free marks' if you build the swap-rewrite habit. INSIGHT: this category trains you for the more advanced 'multi-symbol redefinition' problems where 4-5 operators all change meaning at once.

questions.stem: If 'p × q' means 'p is the father of q', 'p − q' means 'p is the wife of q', and 'p + q' means 'p is the sister of q', then in the relation A × B − C, how is C related to A?

options.option_text: C is the son-in-law of A
C is uncle of A (option here)

questions.explanation: DECODE: A × B → A is father of B (so B is A's child). B − C → B is wife of C (so C is B's husband). LINK: B is A's CHILD and B is C's WIFE → B is A's daughter. Therefore C is A's daughter's husband = SON-IN-LAW. KEY METHOD for symbol-relation chains: draw a small family-tree diagram. A → (parent of) B; B ←(wife)← C. Walk the arrows. EXAM TIP: always identify the GENDER from the relation type — 'father' tells you A is male and B can be any child; 'wife' tells you B is female. If B is female AND A's child, B is A's daughter. PYQ ANGLE: blood-relations-via-symbols is a 5-mark category in IBPS PO Prelims. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests ability to chain operators with semantic constraints (gender, parental relation) — useful in graph/relational reasoning.

questions.stem: If 'a # b' means a + b, and 'a @ b' means a × b, find the value of (5 # 3) @ (4 # 2).
questions.explanation: STEP 1: 5 # 3 = 5 + 3 = 8. STEP 2: 4 # 2 = 4 + 2 = 6. STEP 3: 8 @ 6 = 8 × 6 = 48. KEY METHOD — DEFINE-AND-APPLY: parse innermost parentheses first, then combine outer. Always re-read the operator's definition every time you use it — students lose marks by switching '#' (sum) and '@' (product) mid-solve. EXAM-FAVORITE: SSC, IBPS, RRB all reuse this nested-symbol style — typical 1 Q per Tier 1 paper. SHORTCUT: write the definitions on rough paper as 'a#b = a+b' and 'a@b = a×b' before computing; your eye won't slip back to wrong meanings. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests ability to follow a custom function definition — directly mirrors what you do in programming when calling a user-defined function. INSIGHT: more complex variants use a²+b², a−b², or even a^b — same method, just heavier arithmetic.
